6 Spontaneous Emission: Spontaneous emission is the emission of a photon when a system transits from a higher energy state to a lower energy state without the aid of any external agency. The average life time of the atomic system in the excited state is of the order of 10–8 s. After the life time of the atomic system in the excited state, it comes back to the state of lower energy on its own accord by emitting a photon of energy hf = E2– E1 . In an ordinary light source, the radiation of light from different atoms is not coherent. The radiations are emitted in different directions in random manner. Such type of emission of radiation is called spontaneous emission. The primary advantage of laser scanners is their ability to read barcodes quickly and accurately from a distance, making them indispensable in retail, warehousing, and industrial applications. 1.4.2 Laser printer A laser printer operates based on the principle of electrophotography (xerography), which involves the combined action of electrostatics, photoconductivity, and laser optics to produce printed images. The central component of the printer is a photoconductive drum, usually coated with semiconductor material such as selenium or organic photoconductors. In darkness, this material behaves as an insulator, but when exposed to light it becomes conductive. This property allows a laser beam to selectively remove charge from the drum surface and create an electrostatic image corresponding to the document to be printed. Fine powdered ink called toner, which carries an electric charge, is then attracted to these charged regions and su

ing to the document to be printed. Fine powdered ink called toner, which carries an electric charge, is then attracted to these charged regions and subsequently transferred onto paper. Finally, heat and pressure permanently fix the toner onto the paper, producing the printed output. Steps involved in laser printing: • Charging the drum: A primary charging roller applies a uniform electrostatic charge (usually negative) over the entire surface of the photoconductive drum. • Laser exposure (writing the image): A laser beam, guided by a rotating mirror system, scans across the drum surface. Wherever the laser strikes, the photoconductive surface becomes conductive and the charge is reduced, forming an electrostatic latent image of the document. • Developing the image: Negatively charged toner particles from the toner cartridge are brought near the drum. These particles are attracted to the regions where the charge has been altered by the laser, making the image visible on the drum. • Tran
